To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

halothane and thio-pental bind to GLIC at three trypt-ophan-associated sites, and that binding at the EC domain and EC-TM inter-face disrupts the critical interactions for GLIC gating, destabilizing the open-channel confor-mation that can lead to channel current inhibition.

halothane and thipental bind to three sites on the extracellular (outside of the cell), transmembrane (inside the cell), and extracellular-transmembrane interfaces of a bacterial pentameric liganded ion channel (GLiC) and that the binding disrupts the channel gating mechanism.

halothane and other anesthetics bind to three sites in GLIC, and the binding disrupts the critical interactions for gating and alters the motion of the TM linker, which can lead to channel inhibition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanism of anesthetic binding and action in a bacterial homolog of cns receptors.
the study of the molecular mechanism of anesthetic action in GLIC, the first bacterial pentameric liganded gated ion channel, and its implications in the design of new drugs.
the molecular mechanism of action of general anesthestics in a bacterial homolog of cns receptor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the anesthetics bind to the extracellular domain and to the transmembrane domain and that this binding inhibits channel opening.
the anesthetic binding sites in GLIC are not limited to one or two sites, but rather distributed over the whole protein.
anesthetic binding to GLIC occurs in the EC, TM, and EC-TMD interface, with a higher affinity for thiopental than halothane.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
anesthetic binding in the TM and EC-TM interfaces of GLIC can lead to inhibition.
halothane and other general anesthetics bind to GLIC and inhibit its channel current by binding at multiple sites, including EC domain, EC-TM interface, and TM domain.

the anesthetic binding to GLIC is complex and involves both intra- and inter-subunit sites, with halothane preferentially binding at the intrasubunit site and thiopental preferentially binding at intersubunit site, which is consistent with the anesthetic effects observed in GLIC channel currents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the EC-TM interfaces of the subunits are important sites for general anesthetics to bind to the cys-loop receptors.
halothane and other general anesthetics bind to the EC-TM domain interface, and this binding site is critical for anesthetic actions on the GLIC channel.
halothane binds to multiple sites in GLIC, and the EC-TM binding site is critical to the inhibition of GLIC.
